article.plain_text:
I used the @transitapp for the first time since freshman year yesterday. I thought I was downloading basically the same app I left behind.
But today's Transit App isn't the one I remembered at all. It's a clinic in where startups should look for UX and branding alignment.

I believe everyone has taste. But not every brand gives its taste form well enough. That takes some combination of luck, inspiration, and strategy.
I think the @transitapp team looked in the right place for inspiration: the user. And they've done a remarkable job building a strategy around it.

Every single day, at predictable times, in predictable places, and for similar reasons: millions of time-and-place-data-sharing users.

The hardest data to get legally and they get it pretty much as a birthright from a user base that is:

Homogenous
Gigantic
Predictable
 
Pick your hyperscaler. Platforms that are made for everyone to use for everything/anything. They have to work for datasets that combine those three things; and they churn fast.
Transit is made for everyone too; but to use for one thing and that changes the equation mightily.
If I do one thing really, really well, I actually get to know things about my users cheaply. A product that tries to do many things has no choice but to work harder for the same insights. This can be risky and expensive.
Transit takes easy wins
Maintaining any production app is hard. Maintaining a navigation app at scale is very hard.
Transit squeezes more juice from the fruits of that labor by doing something very easy: they serve users just beyond the call of navigation-app duty, in symbiotic fashion.
It doesn't exactly take a strategy call with Deloitte to be sure that after closing the transit app, users are disproportionately likely to start doomscrolling or playing a game. Prediction is power and that read costs nothing but the calories from breakfast.
Imagine the intrigue when I saw a little tooltip telling me I'm ranked 483rd at my own bus stop.
Only way to climb the food chain: keep pushing adorable emoji containers that ask me about my stop/ride. In other words, put the data in the bag. I was happy to comply because honestly...they made it hard not to.
There's also a counter at the top telling me how many people I've helped just by keeping the app open on my bus. And it increases massively when I do give feedback about my bus/ride.
Transit manages to make taking the bus feel like a communal affair. It is terribly refreshing.
People tend to:
like sharing opinions
love playing games
hate missing the bus
They are already here because we are really, really good at one of those things.
They close our app once positioned at bus/train/stop. They are then very likely to chase 1 or 2.
If we give them 1 and 2 maybe they will help us keep doing 3, and better.
What if we make our app do what they were about to do next anyway?
They gamified the entire transit-riding experience.
Every app doesn't need to be gamified. But this app proves that there are more creative ways to solicit user data than "can we please use this to improve our product?"
Transit app lets me see how my data is helping. Then they made sharing it fun.
An enormous amount of work poured into UI
The buttons are colourful, haptic, and their purpose instantly obvious.
The funky fonts, the exclamation marks, the icons, the ubiquity and customizability of bright colours all over the interface; they all serve a technically sophisticated, strategically ingenious thesis.
Make taking the bus feel like a multiplayer game.
I am thinking of ways I can steal that playbook for what I'm building next.
Hats off and thanks to the @transitapp team.
I will write a more technical case study if I can successfully generalize these principles to my own work next quarter.

article.plain_text:
It's 2018 or so. The NBA finals are starting. LeBron James just led the Cleveland Cavaliers to the NBA finals in one what is still talked about in basketball circles as the greatest individual playoff run of all time.
And here I am, in my third year of University, eating cereal in the computer lab (sue me) and watching @FTFonFS1, when the notorious (and in my eyes visionary) @getnickwright makes the most interesting remark about so-called advanced stats I've ever heard, quoting then-General Manager of the Houston Rockets, Daryl Morey (@dmorey) in the process.
For the uninitiated, advanced stats in basketball work exactly the way researchers at @deepseek_ai develop open-source models, sure, but have evals that are themselves proprietary which help them do what they do. NBA teams like the Rockets or Knicks have in-house statisticians who derive proprietary formulas for them that (try to) distill how "good" a player is into a single number. Think: PER, quarterback rating, or almost every stat in baseball at this point. You put a LOT of metrics or evals in (sports have proxies for what devs call evals), and you get one encompassing number out. Supposedly.
If that sounds familiar, it's because since the dawn of agents as we know them, and indeed before, LLM benchmarks have been trying to do that very thing well.
Sometimes they're decent. Most of the time, they aren't. 
But what do any of these things have to do with each other?
On that spring morning in 2018, probably surrounded by some hectic combination of lecture notes, computer lab goers and half-drunk cans of mountain dew, I heard Wright say, in meaning:
Daryl Morey has a rule for these "advanced stats" the math nerds come up with. If you run the numbers and they have anyone but LeBron James as the best player in the league, the stat is worthless.
What does this have to do with LLM benchmarks? Everything.
By definition, Morey's approach is unscientific. Deciding the observation then judging the merit of the experiment based on that isn't good practice by any reading of a "scientific method".
Wonder how that worked out for Morey.
Morey vs Science
"The scientific method" as a paradigm has served us admirably insofar as we do a decent job quantifying a qualitative thing.
"Size" is qualitative. "Volume" isn't. So we get to have all sorts of agreed-upon truths about size.
We did a good job on that one. It helps also that we can all agree on the formula to get there (l * w * h). More importantly, we all generally agree, for any given set of items, what makes one the biggest; no matter where you went to school, how you'd use the item, whether you happen to sell a competitor to the item, or who's paying to have the set measured and why. Not even if they're also sponsoring open source tape measure research so you can make longer ones. In anticipation of bigger items that very sponsor is likely to produce. Not that such a fantastic scenario would ever happen in the real world.
Sports performance is a little bit different than "bigness" though, isn't it? We don't yet agree on what good looks like the way we agree that 5ml is more than 2. And depending on your roster, "good" in your point guard can change meaning anyway. That makes the job of sports statisticians really hard.
IQ as a proxy for human intellect illustrates this point too. It doesn't not work. It just...doesn't quite work either. Granted, it's useful to group populations sometimes, even if not good enough to sort them (i.e. we can say "if you have 130 IQ or more you're a genius" more easily than we can defend "this 120 IQ engineer will write better code for our frontend team than that 105 IQ one"). *
Intelligence, it would seem, is tricky to resolve so finely.
 
According to this index from BenchLM, Opus 5 is the third most intelligent LLM on the planet. And that's without adjusting for price.
Is the benchmark evidence for this model's quality? Or is its quality (lack thereof) evidence against the benchmark, given the score that such a model achieved?
Every once in a while, a specimen is so clearly at or close to the extremity of a tail that we can normalize around it. Or set it as a standard and use it to check our work.
I find it the best kind of lucky that we seem to agree, all but unanimously, that Opus 5 is almost unusable. Just like Morey was lucky to be in era where it was so obvious who was the best player in the league.
To work, of course, the trick requires an excruciatingly well-qualified subjective judge. To be fair, assumptions always have. But they work terribly well.
Daryl Morey won the NBA Executive of the Year Award in 2018. The quote allegedly was uttered around 2011. Interestingly, before his assumption was essentially a foregone conclusion across his domain. He's also widely considered one of the best-drafting NBA Execs if all time.
There's something to be said for evals and benchmarking. But sometimes, you get a specimen that is so obviously good or so obviously bad that it gives you the rare privilege of having an answer key going into the benchmark test. That specimen, amusingly, becomes the benchmark to your benchmark.
A "standard", if you will.

Conclusion
Perhaps we are lucky Opus 5 is so awful.
I, for one, am a better dev for how thoroughly indifferent I've come to be about benchmarks within the top dozen models in a given class.
Plus, fitting my model, harness, and paradigm (CodeAct-ish vs ReAct-ish) combination to the task like any other part of my dev stack has been an enormous amount of fun; and a lovely return to normalcy that pays for the prep cost in time savings in the long run and vanishingly low inference costs overall.
There are a lot of models out there.  Running and/or tuning my own models fora highly scoped  scoped task me a joy I can only compare in hue to that giddy feeling I used to get when a multi-hundred-line feature  compiles for the fist time.  Due in no small part to the satisfaction of absolutely obliterating a stock model ~50x the size task-for-task. Not that I bother checking lately, to be honest.
Would recommend to one and all.
---
*this of course, assumes that intelligence is all coding requires. and that a frontend dev with more than 100 IQ can exist.

article.plain_text:
Across the tech industry, companies are struggling to find metrics that justify exorbitant amounts of AI spend.
By all the marketing, especially by Magnificent 7, AI primacy is inevitable. By all the numbers, AI adoption doesn't even make cents.
OpenAI and Anthropic have never been profitable businesses. Microsoft's CAPEX on AI and infra is mind bogglingly high. Google went cashflow negative last year for the first time since it went public. To put that in perspective, the president and I shared a surname at the time.
Articles and other media are circling even in mainstream channels raising the alarm that the money around this so-called revolution doesn't add up. It simply doesn't generate enough profit (to hear the intelligent @edzitron say it, any profit) to justify the funds being poured in. And they must continue being poured in at an accelerating rate if American AI wants to maintain what remnants of an edge it has left on Chinese alternatives, which ironically benefit from the hundreds of billions the American economy pours into the training models anyway (ironically, the US imposed sanctions barring them from access to NVIDIA's chips, which landed them all on our side of the curtain, saddled us with the enormous electrical bill the training runs model development commands, and left the product itself wide open for imitation, affording our Chinese peers every opportunity to extract most of the benefit for free that they would happily have paid for anyway). More power to them. American inference would cost a fortune if not for the (very American, as it were) competitive pressure from open models holding their prices down.
The icing on the bitter cake is that AI adoption hasn't yet proven profitable at any kind of scale anyway. At least not for anything that matters. So far, the only thing it's been good at outside of is looking busy and convincing businesses and managers that it can replace human expertise.
Now, the businesses that fell for it are bringing the humans back; with new job titles and bigger salaries, which ironically is technically just AI CAPEX wearing lipstick.
Funny thing: AI is profitable. At least, it can be. Wildly so.
But the tool only works in the hands of someone who knows how to use it, is actually good at the job, and is equipped with exactly the right AI-powered tool
incidentally, programmers happen to combine the first two and can make their own condition 3, and because of that AI has been the closest to profitable in coding of all things. net positive in some small cases like mine, albeit barely as compared to hiring cheap talent. not because it is better at coding than other things because "it's a machine so of course it just 'gets' code". as any half-decent dev will tell you, it actually kind of doesn't. not out of the box anyway.
The world, in real time, is discovering that a hammer and chisel still need Michelangelo to make David. You can't actually replace a craftsman with a tool.
As it turns out, there isn't actually a replacement for people who are actually good at the thing. You can only hope to give them the tools that let them turn that into money for you.
 And it only cost us half the GDP of France since 2022 to find out. G7 country, by the way.
Outstanding work everyone.
Sources
The aforementioned brilliant Ed Zitron (I recommend the entire blog)- https://www.wheresyoured.at/what-happens-if-openai-dies/
A scholar who is more than meets the eye- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eCOxigOJ4Pk
Disclaimers
Unaffiliated (for better or worse) by any of the parties above.

Consider a simple mouse...

They are not formidable in the same way a wolf or lion is.  They are so small, what concern could they present?

If you ever had one in you home, you would know the concern they present.  One mouse can slip into the smallest of cracks or imbalance between door and jam... finding their way to your pantry.

Once they know their entry model, they wait for the optimal time to enter... darkness.  They don't go waltzing in during your time replenishing your stocks of goodies; no... they move in the dark, when your home is still. 

The head of a mouse is all that is required to squeeze into an access point, approximately the diameter of a eraser on a pencil.  Their body is not very large at all.  

This small rodent can destroy a pantry in a short time... I know, we had one years ago... and it avoided glue traps, spring traps and poison.  

That mouse was special forces recon edition.  Just like you are with my concepts.  Large Institutions can't find their way into the small imbalances we can... they have to enter like a backhoe, a big scoop at a time.

We are faster, more nimble and don't require much of a price run to sustain us... like the mouse.

Tip: Paste this Article into you Claude for Personalized Insights.
Grok Bot is SpaceXAI's clearest bet yet that outcomes, not raw model access, are what customers will actually pay for. AI labs are realizing that intelligence alone is becoming harder to differentiate. The problem with selling raw intelligence is that it gets commoditized quickly. Once competing models offer comparable quality at a lower cost, customers have little reason to stay loyal to the model provider itself. The marginal value of raw intelligence is being commoditized faster than the value of systems that apply that intelligence to real-world workflows. You have to keep reinventing yourself to stay in the race, and your customers have no real reason to stick around. They'll switch the moment a better option shows up.
From Copy-Paste to Coding Agents
Back in the caveman days of 2023, if you needed a landing page, you either coded it yourself in VS Code or opened ChatGPT, asked for one section at a time, and stitched it together by hand. That changed when coding agents like Claude Code and Codex arrived in 2025. These agents could write plans, generate code, and update entire projects on their own, something that became possible once models got good at tool calling and driving a terminal, which opened up a lot of new possibilities.
Demand exploded. This is what people had always expected AI to eventually do, the version we'd seen in movies, where you give instructions and it finishes the task. It was a real shift in what people expected from AI. But something was still missing: the sense that these tools could act on their own judgment, not just follow a script.
 
The Accidental Birth of OpenClaw
In 2025, a retired programmer was messing around with AI on the side, working through a handful of personal projects. One of them was an AI agent, and he'd gotten a working prototype together. Then, one weekend, he flew to Marrakesh, Morocco, for a birthday party. The internet there was patchy, but he'd managed to connect his agent to WhatsApp and wanted to try out a few of its features.
While chatting with the bot, he accidentally sent a voice message instead of text. That early prototype had no voice support at all. But the agent still understood it had received an audio file. It downloaded it, converted it to WAV using ffmpeg, ran it through OpenAI's API to transcribe it, and replied on WhatsApp as if nothing unusual had happened. It hadn't been programmed with a voice-message workflow; it simply reasoned its way to a sequence of tools that solved the problem. That moment blew his mind. It became one of the earliest, clearest signs of what these agents were actually capable of.
That prototype was an early version of what became OpenClaw, built by Peter Steinberger. Reuters reports the first version came together in about an hour, something Peter has mentioned in several interviews since.
OpenClaw's Viral Rise and Reality Check
In January 2026, the project exploded. People went wild on X over what the agent could do, using it as a personal assistant to manage email, browse the web, control their computer, and handle everyday tasks. Today, OpenClaw is the sixth most-starred repository on GitHub. It showed that people don't just want a smarter chatbot; they want an assistant that acts on its own.
AI labs took notice of the potential, but Anthropic objected on trademark grounds to the project's original name, Clawdbot, too close to "Claude." The project went through a couple of renames, from Clawdbot to Moltbot and finally to OpenClaw. Since then, its initial hype has cooled off within the AI space. OpenAI later hired Peter to help build its next generation of personal agents.
ChatGPT's website has grown into an agentic environment where you can plug in your whole Google Suite alongside dev tools like GitHub and Supabase, and work with all of it directly from the chat. Codex has kept pace, adding computer use, remote access, plugins, and skills. Anthropic has followed the same path with Claude Cowork, Claude Code, Dispatch, and Claude Tag.
The hype around OpenClaw was real, and interest in autonomous agents hasn't gone anywhere. But endlessly debugging and tweaking a model's behavior gets tedious. It feels productive, but it rarely is. Giving an agent full access to a computer also opened up real security issues. The early hype gave way to a more sober look at the reliability and security problems involved.
Even so, agent-building only accelerated from there. You can see it in where VCs put their money. Y Combinator alone has funded hundreds of AI startups spanning legal, healthcare, and logistics. A striking share of new AI startups are either building agents outright or weaving AI into existing service businesses.
Owning the Outcome
Put all of this together and it tells you where AI labs are headed. People want AI to do everything for them, and they want it secure and reliable. Zoom out and you can see the industry moving toward specialized harnesses built for specific use cases. Every major lab is shifting from selling intelligence to owning outcomes, reducing friction, removing infrastructure hassle, and making the whole thing easier to use.
 
Compute adds another constraint. A single ChatGPT query is already more expensive than a regular Google search, and these long-horizon, autonomous agents need vastly more of it. On top of that, AI labs can't compete with each other, or with the wave of new AI startups, by selling intelligence alone. They need products people will actually pay to keep using.
Enter SpaceXAI
This is where SpaceX comes in. SpaceX, through its relationship with X, xAI, and the wider network of Musk-affiliated companies, had access to a large stream of real-time, human-generated data that most competitors don't. It also had Colossus, one of the largest concentrations of AI compute in the world. What it lacked was a successful product. That changed when it acquired Cursor.
Cursor's strategic problem was that it monetized access to intelligence built by its competitors, paying full API prices for models from Anthropic and OpenAI, while those same labs were subsidizing massive token usage for their own subscribers. SpaceX acquiring Cursor solves that mismatch neatly: massive compute, an existing paying customer base, and a rich stream of usage data, all under one roof. Reportedly, the deal gave SpaceX an unusual choice: acquire Cursor outright for $60 billion, or pay $10 billion instead for a strategic partnership.
You can already see the results of that merger. Grok Bot launched on August 11, 2026. It's a productized, cloud-hosted version of the personal-agent idea OpenClaw popularized, with the ability to spin up bots for specific tasks. SpaceXAI is already cutting the price: Grok Bot originally required a $200 Cursor Ultra subscription or the top Grok tier; within ten days, access had expanded to the $60 Cursor Pro+ plan, the $100 SuperGrok Plus plan, and even standard Cursor team seats.
This is where all that compute pays off. If SpaceXAI can run these agents more cheaply than anyone else, it can put them in front of far more people, apply real pricing pressure on the rest of the field, and stake out a dominant position in the AI race.
The Open-Source Counterweight
 
As the industry's focus shifts to outcomes, though, the moat starts to erode, because this is exactly where open source thrives. New, ambitious projects ship constantly: OpenClaw, Opencode, Pi, DeepSeek Harness. There's also Hermes Agent, which does much of what OpenClaw does while burning far fewer tokens.
Open-source models are competitive now, and cheap. Companies are realizing they don't need the single best model to run their AI workflows. AT&T is one example. It routes AI workloads across models based on capability and cost rather than defaulting to the most powerful model for every task. The company reportedly processes 45 billion tokens a day, and by switching to more cost-effective models where it makes sense, it has cut AI costs by as much as 90%. It routes work based on accuracy, cost, and business value, leaning increasingly on open models as it goes.
We'll likely see more of this over time. It's what keeps the competition honest. So while companies like SpaceXAI race to own the entire stack, open source is steadily making more of that stack interchangeable.
Where This Leaves Us
When the dust settles, we may land in a post-AI-bubble era, not unlike the years that followed the dot-com crash. The hype will fade, but the infrastructure will stay.

AI is the most democratized productivity tool ever created.

AI does not close an ambition gap. 

It rips it wide open.

note_tweet.text:
Plato was actually right..

Researchers proved every LLM on earth is converging on the exact same "universal geometry" of meaning.

They built a method that can translate between ANY model's embeddings without ever seeing the original text or using paired data.

different architectures, different training sets, different parameter counts.. it doesn't matter.

Until now, every AI model has lived in its own isolated mathematical universe.

An embedding vector from Claude meant nothing to GPT, and a vector from Llama meant nothing to Gemini. They spoke entirely different geometric languages.

To bridge them, you always needed paired datasets, complex encoders, or heavy fine-tuning.

Then researchers dropped a bombshell paper.

They built a system that can translate between any model's embeddings without ever seeing the original text, without encoders, and without a single pair of matching data.

How?

Because the geometry is already there.

Different models, built by different companies, with totally different architectures, parameter counts, and training data, are all naturally drifting toward the exact same underlying latent structure of human meaning.

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis isn't just a theory anymore. It’s a mathematical reality.

They built an unsupervised method that maps an unknown embedding from one model straight into a universal representation space, matching text vectors across different models with shockingly high precision.

But here is the dark side nobody is talking about.

If meaning has a universal geometry, and vectors can be freely translated across models without the original text or encoders...

Vector databases are wide open.

An adversary with access only to a company's stored embedding vectors can translate them, invert them, and extract sensitive internal documents, personal data, and proprietary codebases without ever hacking the model itself.
